Classifying objects in Earth orbit with a neural network¶

Course: EAI (Deep Learning), Fontys
Student: Josif Mitsanski

1. Introduction¶

Right now there are tens of thousands of man made objects going around the Earth. The US Space Force tracks them and CelesTrak publishes the list for free. Every object in that list has a type:

Code Meaning
PAY Payload. A satellite, working or dead.
R/B Rocket body. The empty upper stage of the rocket that brought the satellite up.
DEB Debris. Broken pieces, covers, bolts and junk from explosions or collisions.

My question: can a neural network guess the type of an object when it only sees the shape of its orbit and a few facts about the launch?

This matters a bit outside of school too. Space agencies want to know how much junk is up there. When a new object is spotted, somebody has to decide what it is. If orbit numbers alone are enough, that decision could be automated.

Words I use a lot¶

I am new to neural networks, so I am writing down what the words mean in my own language. If a word below shows up later in the notebook, this is what I mean by it.

Word What it means, simply
Feature One piece of information I give the model, like the height of the orbit.
Label or target The answer I want it to predict. Here: is it a satellite, a rocket body or debris.
Training Showing the model examples with the answers, so it can adjust itself to get them right.
Epoch One full pass through all the training examples. Training takes many epochs.
Weights The numbers inside the network that get adjusted during training. This is what the model actually learns.
Loss A score for how wrong the model is. Training tries to make it as small as possible. Lower is better.
Overfitting The model memorised the training examples instead of learning the general rule. It does great on the data it has seen and badly on new data.
Underfitting The opposite. The model is too simple or trained too briefly, so it does badly on everything.
Data leakage I accidentally gave the model a column that contains the answer. The score looks amazing and means nothing.
Class imbalance Some answers are much more common than others. Here, satellites are 9 times more common than rocket bodies.

What I will do¶

  1. Load the CelesTrak catalogue and keep only objects that are still in orbit.
  2. Throw away the columns that would give the answer away (this is important, see section 3).
  3. Build two simple baselines so I have something to compare against.
  4. Build a neural network in Keras.
  5. Test different settings for learning rate and network size and see what happens.
  6. Pick the best model and test it once on data it has never seen.

The short version of the result¶

On the test set the neural network gets 93.7% accuracy and a macro F1 of 0.87. That beats logistic regression (89.8% and 0.74) and it destroys the lazy answer of always guessing the biggest class (57.6% and 0.24).

Satellites and debris are recognised well. Rocket bodies are the hard class, and the model finds most of them but also cries wolf a lot. Section 7 explains why that is a choice I made and not a bug.

2. Dataset¶

Where it comes from¶
Name CelesTrak Satellite Catalog (SATCAT)
Link https://celestrak.org/satcat/
File used https://celestrak.org/pub/satcat.csv
Column docs https://celestrak.org/satcat/satcat-format.php
Downloaded 24 September 2026
Rows 70,793 objects

I downloaded it with the small script scripts/download_satcat.py in this repo. The script puts the date in the filename, because CelesTrak updates the file every day and I want to be able to say exactly which version I used.

Which rows I keep¶

I do not want to use the whole file. I filter it down for three reasons:

  1. Only objects still in orbit. If DECAY_DATE is filled in, the object already burned up in the atmosphere. Its orbit numbers are the last ones measured before it fell, which is a different situation from an object that is still up there. About half the catalogue is already gone, so this removes a lot of rows.
  2. Only things orbiting the Earth. A few hundred rows are probes around the Sun, the Moon or Mars. Their orbit numbers mean something completely different.
  3. No UNK. 168 objects have an unknown type. I cannot train on a label that says "we do not know", so they go.

A quick look at the features¶

Before I choose features I want to see whether the orbit numbers actually differ per class. If the three types have the same orbits, no model will ever work.

What the three types actually are¶

Before looking at numbers it helps to picture what I am trying to tell apart. The catalogue is only a table of numbers, there are no photos in it, so I drew a simple sketch of each type and put a real object from the data underneath it.

The story of one launch explains all three at once. A rocket lifts off carrying a satellite. The satellite is the payload, the part that does a job. The last stage of the rocket lets go of it and stays in orbit as an empty metal tube, the rocket body. Years later something explodes or two objects hit each other, and the pieces become debris.

One real object of each type, straight out of the catalogue:
   OBJECT_NAME OBJECT_TYPE OWNER LAUNCH_DATE  PERIOD  INCLINATION  APOGEE  PERIGEE      RCS
   ISS (ZARYA)         PAY   ISS  1998-11-20   92.95        51.63   422.0    416.0 399.0524
  FALCON 9 R/B         R/B    US  2015-04-27  294.79        25.13 16405.0    183.0  44.4327
FENGYUN 1C DEB         DEB   PRC  1999-05-10  111.03        99.21  1706.0    843.0   0.0391

Takeaway: even these three rows already show the pattern the model will have to learn.

  • The ISS is huge on radar (399 m2) and sits in a low, round orbit. Apogee 422 km and perigee 416 km are almost the same, so the orbit is nearly a circle.
  • The Falcon 9 rocket body has a very stretched orbit. Perigee 183 km but apogee 16,405 km. It dropped its satellite off high up and fell back down on the other side of the orbit, so it is still swinging between those two heights. A period of 295 minutes instead of about 90 comes straight out of that.
  • The Fengyun 1C fragment is tiny, 0.039 m2, and sits at 99 degrees inclination, which is a polar orbit.

That last one has a real story behind it, and it matters for my results later.

In [10]:
fengyun = df.OBJECT_NAME.str.contains('FENGYUN 1C DEB', na=False).sum()
cosmos = df.OBJECT_NAME.str.contains('COSMOS 2251 DEB', na=False).sum()
print(f'pieces of FENGYUN 1C still in orbit : {fengyun:,}')
print(f'pieces of COSMOS 2251 still in orbit: {cosmos:,}')
print(f'together that is {(fengyun + cosmos) / (df.OBJECT_TYPE == "DEB").sum() * 100:.0f}% of all the debris in my data')

pieces of FENGYUN 1C still in orbit : 2,313
pieces of COSMOS 2251 still in orbit: 613
together that is 23% of all the debris in my data

Takeaway: in 2007 China shot down its own weather satellite, Fengyun 1C, as a missile test. That one event produced thousands of fragments and 2,313 of them are still up there today, which is a big chunk of my entire debris class. Cosmos 2251 is the 2009 crash between a dead Russian satellite and an Iridium satellite.

So debris does not arrive one piece at a time. It arrives in families, hundreds or thousands of fragments from a single event, all in very similar orbits because they all started from the same place. I come back to this in the limitations, because it makes my test set easier than real life.

3. Preprocessing¶

3.1 Dropping the columns that cheat¶

This is the part of the project I spent the most time on. Several columns in SATCAT basically contain the answer. If I leave them in, the model gets 99% accuracy and I have learned nothing, because it is just reading the label from another column. This is called data leakage.

Let me show the evidence instead of just claiming it.

In [11]:
name = df.OBJECT_NAME.str.upper()

print('Objects whose NAME contains "DEB":')
print(pd.crosstab(df.OBJECT_TYPE, name.str.contains('DEB', na=False)).loc[order])
print()
print('Objects whose NAME contains "R/B":')
print(pd.crosstab(df.OBJECT_TYPE, name.str.contains('R/B', na=False, regex=False)).loc[order])
print()
print('Objects that have an OPS_STATUS_CODE (percent per class):')
print((pd.crosstab(df.OBJECT_TYPE, df.OPS_STATUS_CODE.notna(), normalize='index') * 100).round(1).loc[order])

Objects whose NAME contains "DEB":
OBJECT_NAME  False  True 
OBJECT_TYPE              
PAY          19967      1
R/B           2299      0
DEB            212  12328

Objects whose NAME contains "R/B":
OBJECT_NAME  False  True 
OBJECT_TYPE              
PAY          19952     16
R/B             53   2246
DEB          12461     79

Objects that have an OPS_STATUS_CODE (percent per class):
OPS_STATUS_CODE  False  True 
OBJECT_TYPE                  
PAY                7.2   92.8
R/B               99.9    0.1
DEB              100.0    0.0

So:

  • OBJECT_NAME literally spells out the class. Almost every debris object has "DEB" in its name and almost every rocket body has "R/B". A model reading the name is doing text matching, not learning.
  • OPS_STATUS_CODE is filled in for 93% of payloads and for basically nothing else. Only a working satellite has an operational status, so this column says "I am a payload".
  • OBJECT_ID is the launch designator like 1998-067A. The letter suffix counts up per launch, so a piece of debris from the 900th fragment has a long suffix and a payload usually has a single letter. Again a giveaway.
  • NORAD_CAT_ID is a counter, so it is mostly just launch year in disguise, plus the same fragment numbering pattern.
  • DECAY_DATE is empty for every row I kept, so it carries no information at all now.

All of these get dropped. ORBIT_CENTER also goes because after filtering it is EA for every row.

3.2 A column that turned out to be useless¶

I planned to use ORBIT_TYPE as a feature. When I actually checked it, it was not usable.

In [12]:
print(df.ORBIT_TYPE.value_counts())

ORBIT_TYPE
ORB    34807
Name: count, dtype: int64

Every remaining object has ORB. A column with only one value cannot help a model separate anything, so I drop it too. Small lesson learned: check your features before you trust your plan.

3.3 The missing RCS values¶

RCS (radar cross section, how big the object looks to radar) is missing for a lot of rows. Before deciding what to do, I checked whether it is missing at random, because that changes the right answer.

Takeaway: this was the most interesting thing I found while exploring. RCS is not missing randomly at all. It is missing for 100% of objects launched since 2020 and for almost none launched before 2010. CelesTrak simply does not publish a size for the newer objects yet.

It looks like RCS missing means "it is a satellite" (82% of payloads have no RCS), but that is a side effect: most new objects are satellites, and all new objects have no RCS. The real driver is age, not type.

What I do about it: I fill the missing values with the median of the training set, and I add an extra column rcs_missing that is 1 when the value was filled in. That way the network knows the number is a guess instead of silently believing a fake value. Later in the baseline section I check whether that flag actually matters.

3.4 Rows with no orbit data¶

A few hundred old objects have no period, apogee, perigee or inclination at all. That is four of my seven numeric features missing at once, so imputing them would be inventing the whole row. There are only 329 of them out of 34,800, so I just drop those rows.

In [15]:
before = len(df)
df = df.dropna(subset=['PERIOD', 'INCLINATION', 'APOGEE', 'PERIGEE', 'LAUNCH_YEAR'])
print(f'dropped {before - len(df)} rows with no orbit data ({(before-len(df))/before*100:.1f}%)')
print(f'{len(df)} rows left for modelling')
df = df.reset_index(drop=True)

dropped 333 rows with no orbit data (1.0%)
34474 rows left for modelling

3.5 Building the feature table¶

Numeric features. Period, apogee and perigee cover an enormous range. Perigee can be 300 km and apogee can be 640,000 km. If I feed those in raw, the huge values dominate everything. So I take log10 of them first, which squashes the range without losing the ordering. RCS gets the same treatment because it goes from 0.0001 to 830 m2.

Categorical features. OWNER has 106 different values and LAUNCH_SITE has 34. Most of them appear only a handful of times. Making a column for each would add a lot of nearly empty columns, which is a good way to overfit. So I keep the categories that appear at least 100 times in the training set and call the rest OTHER, then one hot encode.

One hot encoding means: instead of one column "OWNER" with text in it, I make one column per owner that is 1 or 0. A neural network can only work with numbers, and if I just numbered the owners 1 to 106 the network would think owner 50 is somehow bigger than owner 10.

In [16]:
def build_features(data, top_owners, top_sites):
    """Turn the cleaned catalogue into a numeric feature table."""
    X = pd.DataFrame(index=data.index)

    # numbers, log scaled where the range is huge
    X['log_period']  = np.log10(data.PERIOD)
    X['inclination'] = data.INCLINATION
    X['log_apogee']  = np.log10(data.APOGEE + 1)
    X['log_perigee'] = np.log10(data.PERIGEE + 1)
    X['launch_year'] = data.LAUNCH_YEAR
    X['rcs_missing'] = data.RCS.isna().astype(int)
    X['log_rcs']     = np.log10(data.RCS)      # stays NaN where missing, filled after the split

    # categories, rare ones grouped into OTHER
    owner = data.OWNER.where(data.OWNER.isin(top_owners), 'OTHER')
    site  = data.LAUNCH_SITE.where(data.LAUNCH_SITE.isin(top_sites), 'OTHER')

    return pd.concat([
        X,
        pd.get_dummies(owner, prefix='own').astype(float),
        pd.get_dummies(site,  prefix='site').astype(float),
    ], axis=1)

3.6 Splitting the data¶

I split into 70% train, 15% validation and 15% test, and I use stratify so all three splits have the same class mix. Without that, a random split could easily give the test set too few rocket bodies to measure anything.

What each part is for:

  • Train is what the network learns from.
  • Validation is what I look at while tuning. Early stopping watches it and I compare experiments on it.
  • Test I touch exactly once, at the very end. If I tuned on the test set, my final number would be optimistic and meaningless.

Two things happen after the split on purpose:

  • the list of common owners and launch sites is taken from the training set only
  • the median used to fill missing RCS is the training median
  • the scaler is fitted on the training set only

If I computed any of those on the full data, information from validation and test would leak into training and my scores would be too good.

In [17]:
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

CLASSES = ['PAY', 'R/B', 'DEB']
LABEL_TO_INT = {c: i for i, c in enumerate(CLASSES)}


def make_dataset(data, seed=SEED):
    """Split, encode and scale. Returns a dict with the ready to use arrays."""
    y = data.OBJECT_TYPE.map(LABEL_TO_INT).values
    idx = np.arange(len(data))

    i_train, i_rest = train_test_split(idx, test_size=0.30, stratify=y, random_state=seed)
    i_val, i_test   = train_test_split(i_rest, test_size=0.50, stratify=y[i_rest], random_state=seed)

    train_rows = data.iloc[i_train]
    top_owners = train_rows.OWNER.value_counts()[lambda s: s >= 100].index.tolist()
    top_sites  = train_rows.LAUNCH_SITE.value_counts()[lambda s: s >= 100].index.tolist()

    X = build_features(data, top_owners, top_sites)
    X['log_rcs'] = X.log_rcs.fillna(X.iloc[i_train].log_rcs.median())

    scaler = StandardScaler().fit(X.iloc[i_train].values)

    out = {'columns': list(X.columns), 'n_features': X.shape[1],
           'top_owners': top_owners, 'top_sites': top_sites}
    for part, rows in [('train', i_train), ('val', i_val), ('test', i_test)]:
        out['X_' + part] = scaler.transform(X.iloc[rows].values)
        out['y_' + part] = y[rows]
    return out


data = make_dataset(df)

print(f"features: {data['n_features']}")
print(f"train {len(data['y_train'])} | validation {len(data['y_val'])} | test {len(data['y_test'])}")
print(f"owners kept: {len(data['top_owners'])} | launch sites kept: {len(data['top_sites'])}")
print()
print('class mix per split (%):')
mix = pd.DataFrame({p: pd.Series(data['y_' + p]).value_counts(normalize=True) * 100
                    for p in ['train', 'val', 'test']}).round(1)
mix.index = [CLASSES[i] for i in mix.index]
print(mix)

Takeaway: 31 features and the class mix is identical in all three splits, so the stratified split did its job. Scaling means every feature now has mean 0 and standard deviation 1, which matters for neural networks because otherwise launch_year (around 2000) would swamp inclination (0 to 180) just because its numbers are bigger.

3.7 Do my features repeat each other?¶

Now that the features exist I should check whether some of them are basically saying the same thing twice. Two features that always move together carry one piece of information, not two.

The measure for this is correlation. It runs from +1 to -1:

  • +1 means when one goes up the other always goes up too
  • 0 means they have nothing to do with each other
  • -1 means when one goes up the other always goes down

I only check this on the training set, same rule as everywhere else, and only for the seven number features. The one hot columns are all 0 or 1 so correlation does not say much about them.

pairs = (corr.abs()
         .where(np.triu(np.ones(corr.shape), 1).astype(bool))
         .stack().sort_values(ascending=False))

print('The strongest relationships between my features:')
for (a, b), _ in pairs.head(5).items():
    print(f'  {a:12s} and {b:12s}  correlation {corr.loc[a, b]:+.2f}')

The strongest relationships between my features:
  log_period   and log_apogee    correlation +0.95
  log_period   and log_perigee   correlation +0.83
  launch_year  and rcs_missing   correlation +0.80
  log_apogee   and log_perigee   correlation +0.76
  log_period   and inclination   correlation -0.60

Takeaway: two pairs stand out, and both of them have a real world reason behind them.

1. Period and apogee, correlation +0.95. These are almost the same feature. That is not a coincidence in the data, it is physics. Kepler's third law says how long an orbit takes is decided by how big the orbit is. So if I know how high something flies, I already know roughly how long it takes to go around. Perigee is in the same family at +0.83.

2. Launch year and rcs_missing, correlation +0.80. This is the number that proves what I suspected back in section 3.3. The flag for "RCS was missing" is 80% the same thing as "this was launched recently". It is not secret extra knowledge, it is launch year wearing a hat.

Does this hurt? For a neural network, not really. Unlike a linear model, it does not fall apart when two inputs overlap, it just learns smaller weights for both. That is also exactly what I measured in section 4: removing the rcs_missing flag changed macro F1 by 0.007, which is nothing.

So why check at all? Two reasons. It tells me my 31 features are not 31 independent facts, more like 25, so I should not expect a bigger network to keep finding new things forever. And it warns me not to say things like "period is the most important feature", because apogee would do almost the same job on its own.

One more thing worth noticing: period and inclination have a correlation of -0.60. Things in high, slow orbits tend to sit near the equator, and things in fast low orbits are more often in steep polar orbits. That is not physics forcing it, that is just how humans use space.

4. Baselines¶

Before building a neural network I need something to compare against. A fancy model that cannot beat a dumb model is not worth anything. I use two baselines:

  1. Majority class. Always answer PAY. This shows what accuracy is worth nothing.
  2. Logistic regression. A simple, fast, linear model from scikit learn. If the neural network cannot beat this, the extra complexity is not justified.

How I measure "good", in plain words¶

Accuracy is just the share of answers that were right. It is the obvious choice and it is misleading here. Rocket bodies are only 6.5% of the data, so a model can ignore them completely and still score well. I need something that notices that.

Three words I use from here on. Imagine the model just said "this is a rocket body":

  • Precision answers when it says R/B, how often is it right? Low precision means it cries wolf.
  • Recall answers of all the real rocket bodies out there, how many did it find? Low recall means it misses things.
  • F1 squashes those two into one number. It is only high when both are decent, so a model cannot cheat it by being good at one and terrible at the other.

You usually have to trade one for the other. A model that shouts "rocket body" at everything has perfect recall and awful precision. A model that only says it when completely certain has the opposite problem.

Macro F1 is the F1 of each of the three classes, averaged with equal weight. Equal weight is the important bit: the tiny rocket body class counts exactly as much as the huge payload class, so a model that ignores rocket bodies gets punished hard. That is the number I use to compare everything in this notebook.

In [20]:
from sklearn.dummy import DummyClassifier
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score, f1_score, classification_report, confusion_matrix

def score(y_true, y_pred):
    return accuracy_score(y_true, y_pred), f1_score(y_true, y_pred, average='macro')

majority = DummyClassifier(strategy='most_frequent').fit(data['X_train'], data['y_train'])
logreg   = LogisticRegression(max_iter=2000, random_state=SEED).fit(data['X_train'], data['y_train'])

rows = []
for name, model in [('Majority class', majority), ('Logistic regression', logreg)]:
    acc, f1 = score(data['y_val'], model.predict(data['X_val']))
    rows.append({'model': name, 'val accuracy': round(acc, 3), 'val macro F1': round(f1, 3)})

baseline_results = pd.DataFrame(rows)
print(baseline_results.to_string(index=False))

5. The neural network¶
How I think about it¶
A neural network here is a stack of layers. Each layer takes the numbers from the layer before,
multiplies them by weights, adds a bias and passes the result through an activation function.
Training means: make a guess, measure how wrong it is, and nudge every weight a little in the
direction that makes the error smaller. Do that thousands of times.


My choices and the reason for each:






Choice
What I picked
Why






Input
31 numbers
one per feature after scaling and one hot encoding




Hidden layers
Dense + ReLU
ReLU is the normal default, it is fast and does not suffer from vanishing gradients the way sigmoid does




Output
3 neurons + softmax
one per class, softmax turns the outputs into probabilities that add up to 1




Loss
sparse categorical crossentropy
the standard loss for multi class problems, "sparse" because my labels are 0/1/2 instead of one hot




Optimiser
Adam
adapts the step size per weight, works well without much tuning




Batch size
256
big enough to be fast, small enough to still update often




Early stopping
patience 8 on validation loss
stops when the validation loss has not improved for 8 epochs and puts back the best weights, so I do not have to guess the right number of epochs






Class weights¶
Rocket bodies are 6.5% of the data. Without help, the network learns that ignoring them costs
almost nothing. Class weights fix that by making a mistake on a rare class count more in the
loss. With balanced weights, a rocket body error counts about 5 times more than a payload error.


















In [23]:






from sklearn.utils.class_weight import compute_class_weight


def class_weights_for(y_train):
    """Weight each class by how rare it is, so the rare classes are not ignored."""
    weights = compute_class_weight('balanced', classes=np.arange(3), y=y_train)
    return dict(enumerate(weights))


weights = class_weights_for(data['y_train'])

print('class weights used in training:')
for i, c in enumerate(CLASSES):
    print(f'  {c:4s} {weights[i]:.2f}')

























class weights used in training:
  PAY  0.58
  R/B  5.12
  DEB  0.93

























One function for every experiment¶
To compare hyperparameters fairly, every model has to be built the same way. So I write one
build_model(params) function and every experiment later calls it with a different dictionary.
Nothing else changes between runs, which means any difference I see really comes from the
hyperparameter and not from me accidentally changing something else.


















In [24]:






def build_model(params, n_features, n_classes=3, seed=SEED):
    """Build one MLP. params: hidden_layers (list of ints), learning_rate, dropout."""
    keras.utils.set_random_seed(seed)          # same starting weights every time

    model = keras.Sequential(name='mlp')
    model.add(keras.layers.Input(shape=(n_features,)))
    for units in params['hidden_layers']:
        model.add(keras.layers.Dense(units, activation='relu'))
        if params.get('dropout', 0) > 0:
            model.add(keras.layers.Dropout(params['dropout']))
    model.add(keras.layers.Dense(n_classes, activation='softmax'))

    model.compile(
        optimizer=keras.optimizers.Adam(learning_rate=params['learning_rate']),
        loss='sparse_categorical_crossentropy',
        metrics=['accuracy'])
    return model


def train_model(params, ds, seed=SEED, max_epochs=150, patience=8, use_class_weights=True):
    """Train one model and return it together with its history.

    The class weights are always taken from the dataset that is passed in, so an
    experiment on a different dataset still gets the weights that belong to it.
    """
    model = build_model(params, ds['n_features'], seed=seed)
    stop = keras.callbacks.EarlyStopping(monitor='val_loss', patience=patience,
                                         restore_best_weights=True)
    history = model.fit(
        ds['X_train'], ds['y_train'],
        validation_data=(ds['X_val'], ds['y_val']),
        epochs=max_epochs, batch_size=256,
        class_weight=class_weights_for(ds['y_train']) if use_class_weights else None,
        callbacks=[stop], verbose=0)
    return model, history

def plot_curves(history, title, filename=None):
    """Draw training and validation loss and accuracy for one run."""
    h = history.history
    epochs = range(1, len(h['loss']) + 1)
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.4))
    ax[0].plot(epochs, h['loss'], label='train')
    ax[0].plot(epochs, h['val_loss'], label='validation')
    ax[0].set_title('Loss')
    ax[0].set_xlabel('Epoch')
    ax[0].set_ylabel('Loss')
    ax[0].legend()
    ax[1].plot(epochs, h['accuracy'], label='train')
    ax[1].plot(epochs, h['val_accuracy'], label='validation')
    ax[1].set_title('Accuracy')
    ax[1].set_xlabel('Epoch')
    ax[1].set_ylabel('Accuracy')
    ax[1].legend()
    fig.suptitle(title)
    plt.tight_layout()
    if filename:
        plt.savefig(filename, dpi=130)
    plt.show()

The two ways training can go wrong¶
Before I start changing settings I want to be clear about what I am looking for in a learning
curve, because almost every choice later comes back to these two problems.


Underfitting means the model is too weak, or trained too briefly. It never picked up the
pattern. You see it when the training loss and the validation loss are both high and sitting
close together. The model is equally bad everywhere, which means it never learned much.


Overfitting means the model started memorising the training rows instead of learning the
general rule. You see it when the training loss keeps falling but the validation loss turns
around and starts rising. It is getting better at the data it has already seen and worse at
everything else, which is the opposite of useful.


Rather than just describe this, I want to see it. So I run my biggest network twice with early
stopping switched off, for a fixed 150 epochs:


    

  • Left: on the full training set, 24,131 objects.
    • 

  • Right: on only 1,000 objects. Less data to learn from makes memorising much easier, so this
is the usual way to force overfitting on purpose.
    • 



















In [28]:






BIG = {'hidden_layers': [256, 128, 64], 'learning_rate': 0.001, 'dropout': 0.0}

def train_without_early_stopping(X, y, epochs=150, batch_size=256):
    """Train for a fixed number of epochs with nothing to stop it going too far."""
    model = build_model(BIG, data['n_features'])
    return model.fit(X, y, validation_data=(data['X_val'], data['y_val']),
                     epochs=epochs, batch_size=batch_size,
                     class_weight=class_weights_for(y), verbose=0).history

# the full training set
full_history = train_without_early_stopping(data['X_train'], data['y_train'])

# a deliberately tiny slice of it
rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED)
small = rng.choice(len(data['X_train']), 1000, replace=False)
small_history = train_without_early_stopping(data['X_train'][small], data['y_train'][small],
                                             batch_size=64)

for name, h in [('full training set (24,131 rows)', full_history), ('only 1,000 rows', small_history)]:
    best = int(np.argmin(h['val_loss']))
    print(f'{name}:')
    print(f'    best validation loss {h["val_loss"][best]:.4f} at epoch {best + 1}')
    print(f'    at epoch 150: training loss {h["loss"][-1]:.4f}, validation loss {h["val_loss"][-1]:.4f}')
    print(f'    validation loss got {h["val_loss"][-1] - h["val_loss"][best]:+.4f} worse after its best point')

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11.5, 4))

          (small_history, 'Only 1,000 rows: classic overfitting')]

for ax, (h, title) in zip(axes, panels):
    epochs = range(1, len(h['loss']) + 1)
    best = int(np.argmin(h['val_loss']))
    ax.plot(epochs, h['loss'], label='training loss')
    ax.plot(epochs, h['val_loss'], label='validation loss')
    ax.axvline(best + 1, color='grey', ls='--', lw=1)

    ax.legend(fontsize=8)

axes[0].set_ylabel('Loss (lower is better)')
axes[1].annotate('validation loss climbing\nwhile training loss falls\nis what overfitting looks like',
                 xy=(110, small_history['val_loss'][109]),
                 xytext=(45, small_history['val_loss'][109] + 0.12),
                 arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle='->', color='dimgrey'), fontsize=8.5, color='dimgrey')
fig.suptitle('The same network on a lot of data and on very little data (no early stopping)')
plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('../images/overfitting_demo.png', dpi=130)
plt.show()
















































Takeaway: the right hand chart is the textbook picture. Validation loss drops for about 16
epochs, hits its best point, then climbs and keeps climbing, while the training loss slides all
the way down towards zero. By epoch 150 the network knows those 1,000 objects almost perfectly
and has become noticeably worse at everything else. That is memorising, not learning. The dashed
line is where early stopping would have pulled it out.


But the left hand chart surprised me, and it is the more useful result. On the full training
set the same network hardly overfits at all across 150 epochs. The two lines drift apart a
little and that is it. The validation loss does not run away.


The reason is simply that 24,131 examples is a lot for a problem with 31 features. There are too
many different objects for the network to memorise them one by one, so the cheapest thing it can
do is actually learn the rule.


This explains something that comes later. In Experiment C I add dropout to fight overfitting
and it makes the model worse. The left hand chart is why: on the full data there was not much
overfitting to fight. Dropout was a cure for an illness this model did not really have, so all
it did was take away capacity the network was still using.


And it explains why early stopping is enough here. It quietly picks the best epoch for me, so
I never have to guess how long to train, and that turned out to be all the protection this model
needed.

Starlink satellites in or out of the data
best settings from A and B






I only change one thing at a time. If I changed two, I would not know which one caused
the difference.




Note on running time. Each of the four experiment cells below trains 6 to 12 networks, so
it takes roughly 2 to 3 minutes. Training itself is silent (verbose=0) to keep the notebook
readable, so each run prints one short line when it finishes. If you see those lines appearing,
it is working. The whole notebook takes about 12 minutes on a laptop without a GPU.




Making the results trustworthy¶
A neural network starts with random weights, so two runs with the same settings give slightly
different numbers. If I ran each setting once, I could easily call a setting "better" when it
was just lucky. So I run every setting three times with three different seeds and report
the average and the spread. The spread tells me whether a difference is real or just noise.


















In [30]:






import time

SEEDS = [42, 7, 2024]


def run_experiment(name, setting, params, ds=None, seeds=SEEDS, use_class_weights=True):
    """Train the same settings once per seed and return the averaged result plus the histories."""
    ds = data if ds is None else ds
    accs, f1s, epochs, histories = [], [], [], []

    for seed in seeds:
        started = time.time()
        model, history = train_model(params, ds, seed=seed, use_class_weights=use_class_weights)
        pred = model.predict(ds['X_val'], verbose=0).argmax(axis=1)
        acc, f1 = score(ds['y_val'], pred)
        accs.append(acc)
        f1s.append(f1)
        epochs.append(len(history.history['loss']))
        histories.append(history)
        # one short line per run, so I can see it is still working during the long cells
        print(f'  {setting:22s} seed {seed:<5d} acc {acc:.4f}  macro F1 {f1:.4f}'
              f'  ({epochs[-1]} epochs, {time.time() - started:.0f}s)', flush=True)

    return {
        'experiment': name,
        'setting': setting,
        'val accuracy': np.mean(accs),
        'acc spread': np.std(accs),
        'val macro F1': np.mean(f1s),
        'F1 spread': np.std(f1s),
        'epochs': int(np.mean(epochs)),
        'histories': histories,
        'params': params,
    }


def results_table(runs):
    """Turn a list of runs into a readable table."""
    table = pd.DataFrame([{k: r[k] for k in
                           ['experiment', 'setting', 'val accuracy', 'acc spread',
                            'val macro F1', 'F1 spread', 'epochs']} for r in runs])
    return table.round({'val accuracy': 4, 'acc spread': 4, 'val macro F1': 4, 'F1 spread': 4})


def plot_experiment(runs, title, filename, seed_index=0):
    """One panel per setting showing train and validation loss of the first seed."""
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, len(runs), figsize=(3.4 * len(runs), 3.2), sharey=True)
    axes = np.atleast_1d(axes)
    for ax, run in zip(axes, runs):
        h = run['histories'][seed_index].history
        epochs = range(1, len(h['loss']) + 1)
        ax.plot(epochs, h['loss'], label='train')
        ax.plot(epochs, h['val_loss'], label='validation')
        ax.set_title(f"{run['setting']}\nval acc {run['val accuracy']:.3f}", fontsize=10)
        ax.set_xlabel('Epoch')
    axes[0].set_ylabel('Loss')
    axes[0].legend(fontsize=8)
    fig.suptitle(title)
    plt.tight_layout()
    plt.savefig(filename, dpi=130)
    plt.show()

























Experiment A: learning rate¶
The learning rate decides how big a step the optimiser takes each time it updates the weights.
Too big and it jumps over the good solution and never settles. Too small and it crawls, and
early stopping may cut it off before it arrives. I test four values, each one ten times smaller
than the last.

Takeaway: the learning rate matters a lot and the pattern is the classic one. The biggest
value is unstable, the loss curve bounces around because every step overshoots. The smallest
value learns smoothly but too slowly, so early stopping ends the run before it has caught up.
The middle values win. The error bars also show the unstable setting has a much bigger spread
between seeds, which is another sign that it is not reliable.






















Experiment B: network size¶
Now I keep the learning rate at 0.001 and change how many neurons the network has. More neurons
means more weights, so the network can learn more complicated patterns, but it can also start
memorising the training data instead of learning the general rule.

small (16)             best epoch 149 | train loss 0.2374 | val loss 0.2559 | gap +0.0185
medium (64, 32)        best epoch  98 | train loss 0.1629 | val loss 0.1832 | gap +0.0203
large (256, 128, 64)   best epoch  77 | train loss 0.1158 | val loss 0.1714 | gap +0.0556




































Takeaway: bigger is better here, but it is not free.


The small network is clearly too weak. It runs into the epoch limit without ever catching up,
so 16 neurons simply cannot hold the patterns that separate three classes.


The large network wins on validation macro F1, and it also gets there in about half as many
epochs as the medium one. But look at the gap chart: the distance between validation loss and
training loss is roughly three times bigger for the large network. That gap is the
fingerprint of overfitting, the model is starting to learn things that are only true about the
training rows.


So the large network is at the point where it is still gaining more than it is memorising, but
it is the closest one to the edge. That is exactly the situation where dropout is supposed to
help, so that is the next experiment.






















Experiment C: dropout on the large network¶
Dropout randomly switches off a percentage of the neurons during each training step. The network
cannot rely on one single neuron to carry a feature, so it has to spread the job around. That
usually makes it generalise better. I only apply it to the large network, because that is the one
showing the overfitting gap.

In [38]:






plot_experiment(dropout_runs, 'Experiment C: effect of dropout on the large network',
                '../images/exp_dropout.png')
















































Takeaway: dropout made it worse, and I did not expect that.


Macro F1 drops from about 0.88 with no dropout, to 0.86 at 0.2, to 0.85 at 0.4. The spread
between seeds is only about 0.006 to 0.012, so these differences are several times bigger than
the noise. This is a real effect, not luck.


Why did the standard fix for overfitting not help? My reading is that the large network was not
actually overfitting badly yet. Early stopping was already doing that job: it stops the run at
the epoch where validation loss is lowest, before the memorising has time to hurt. Dropout on
top of that just throws away capacity the network was still using, so it underfits instead. The
curves back that up, the runs with dropout have the training and validation lines glued together,
which looks tidy but at a worse loss.


Lesson: a regularisation technique is a cure for a specific illness. Adding it because it is
famous, without first checking that the illness is there, can make the model worse. If I had run
only this experiment and not the size experiment, I would have had no idea why.

So the honest summary is: the difference between my worst sensible setting and my best one is
about 5 points of macro F1, while the difference between the broken setting and the rest is
about 20 points. Getting hyperparameters into the right ballpark matters a lot. Polishing them
inside that ballpark matters much less than the data work in section 3 did.

More than half of all the payloads in orbit are Starlink satellites. They were all launched
recently, they all sit in almost the same orbit and they are all owned by US. So a big part of
what my model calls "recognising a satellite" could really be "recognising a Starlink".


To find out, I rebuild the whole dataset without Starlink and train the same model on it.

In [43]:






plot_experiment(starlink_runs, 'Bonus: the same model trained with and without Starlink',
                '../images/exp_starlink.png')
















































Takeaway: the two metrics disagree, and that is the interesting part.


Accuracy drops from about 0.936 to 0.919. Macro F1 barely moves, from about 0.874 to
0.868, which is about the same size as the spread between seeds, so I cannot call that a real
drop.


Why the difference? Starlink satellites are 56% of the payload class and they are extremely easy
to classify: thousands of near identical objects, same owner, same launch years, almost the same
orbit. Accuracy counts every row equally, so a big block of easy rows pushes it up. Macro F1
gives each of the three classes the same weight, so it does not care that one class got easier.


Removing Starlink also flips the class balance completely: debris becomes the biggest class at
53% and payloads drop to 37%. So the two runs are not only different in difficulty, they are
different problems.


What I take from this: my headline accuracy of about 94% is partly a gift from one mega
constellation. Macro F1 is the number I should quote, because it survived the test.






















7. Final evaluation on the test set¶
Everything above was decided using the validation set. Now I take the settings that scored the
best macro F1, train that model, and run it on the test set. This is the first and only time
the test data is used. That is the whole point: the number it gives me is what I would expect on
new objects, because nothing about those rows influenced any of my choices.


















In [44]:

print(f"  learning rate : {BEST_PARAMS['learning_rate']}")

print(f"  validation macro F1 was {best['val macro F1']:.4f}")

test_pred = final_model.predict(data['X_test'], verbose=0).argmax(axis=1)

Confusion matrix¶
A confusion matrix shows exactly which classes get mixed up with which. Rows are the true type,
columns are what the model guessed. Everything on the diagonal is correct.


I show it twice: raw counts, and normalised per row. The normalised one is easier to read here
because the classes have very different sizes.

sns.heatmap(cm_norm, annot=True, fmt='.2f', cmap='Blues', cbar=False, vmin=0, vmax=1,
            xticklabels=CLASSES, yticklabels=CLASSES, ax=axes[1])
axes[1].set_title('Confusion matrix, share of each true class')
axes[1].set_xlabel('Predicted type')
axes[1].set_ylabel('True type')

plt.tight_layout()
plt.savefig('../images/confusion_matrix.png', dpi=130)
plt.show()

Reading the confusion matrix¶
PAY (satellites). Almost all of them are found. The few mistakes mostly get called R/B. That
makes sense, a big satellite in a high orbit looks a lot like a spent upper stage from the outside.


DEB (debris). Also very good. Debris is small on radar and sits in messy high inclination
orbits left over from explosions, which is a clear signature.


R/B (rocket bodies). This is where the model struggles, and the two matrices tell different
halves of the story:


    

  • Recall is high. Looking at the R/B row, the model catches most real rocket bodies. That is
the class weights doing their work.
    • 

  • Precision is low. Looking at the R/B column, a lot of the things it calls R/B are actually
payloads or debris. Because payloads are nine times more common than rocket bodies, even a small
percentage of payloads leaking into that column outnumbers the real rocket bodies.
    • 



This is a trade off, not a bug. I chose it when I turned on class weights. Without them the model
would find only a third of the rocket bodies but be more trustworthy when it did say R/B. Which
one is better depends on what you want: if you are surveying how much junk is in a given orbit,
catching them all matters more. If a human has to check every alert, precision matters more.


The physical reason the class is hard is simple. A rocket body is the thing that delivered the
payload, so it starts in a very similar orbit to the satellite it launched. From orbit numbers
alone, the two are genuinely close.






















8. Discussion and limitations¶
What worked¶
    

  • Removing the leaky columns. This was the single most important decision in the project. With
OBJECT_NAME left in, the task is string matching and the result is meaningless.
    • 

  • Class weights. Rocket body recall went from 0.32 to above 0.9. Worth the precision it cost.
    • 

  • Log scaling the wide numeric features. Apogee ranges over five orders of magnitude and the
network handles it much better after log10.
    • 

  • Checking the missing values instead of guessing. I nearly imputed RCS with the median and
moved on. Finding out that it is missing by launch date and not at random changed how I explain
the whole feature.
    • 



Limitations, the honest list¶
    

  1. The test set is not really "new objects". It is a random slice of the same catalogue. Debris
comes in families, one explosion makes hundreds of fragments with almost the same orbit. A random
split can put siblings from the same event in both train and test, which makes the job easier
than real life. Splitting by launch event or by year would be a harder and fairer test.
    2. 

  2. Starlink flatters the accuracy. 56% of the payload class is one near identical group that
is very easy to recognise. The bonus experiment showed accuracy drops from 0.936 to 0.919 when
I remove them, while macro F1 barely moves. So my accuracy number is partly a gift from one
mega constellation, and macro F1 is the more honest headline.
    3. 

  3. One snapshot in time. The catalogue changes daily. A model trained on today's data would
probably do worse on objects launched in five years, because launch patterns keep changing.
    4. 

  4. Rocket body precision is low. Useful for a survey, annoying for anything that needs a human
to follow up on every alert.
    5. 

  5. I only tested a small grid by hand. Four learning rates, three sizes and three dropout values
is not a real search. Something like random search or Keras Tuner would cover more ground.
    6. 

  6. A neural network may not even be the right tool here. The features are a small table of
numbers and categories, which is exactly where gradient boosted trees usually win. I did not try
one because the assignment is about neural networks, but I would expect it to be competitive.
    7. 



What I would do next¶
    

  • Split by launch year instead of randomly, and see how much the score drops.
    • 

  • Try XGBoost or a random forest as a third baseline.
    • 

  • Look at which features the model actually relies on, with permutation importance.
    • 

  • Try treating R/B against everything else as a two class problem, since that is where the errors are.
    •
